Question: A frog makes \(3\) jumps, each exactly \(1\) meter long. The directions of the jumps are chosen independently and at random. What is the probability that the frog’s final position is no more than \(1\) meter from its starting position?
Solution:
Assume the conventional model: the frog moves in the plane, and each jump direction is independently uniform over a full circle. Let \(O,A,B\) be its starting position and its positions after the first two jumps. Write \(\theta\) for the smaller angle between the first two jump directions, measured in radians. Folding a uniform full-circle angle into its smaller angle makes \(\theta\) uniform on \([0,\pi]\).

For \(0<\theta<\pi\), triangle \(OAB\) has \(OA=AB=1\) and angle \(\pi-\theta\) at \(A\). Its equal base angles are therefore \(\theta/2\).

The third endpoint lies on the unit circle centered at \(B\). It is successful exactly when it also lies inside or on the unit circle centered at \(O\). These two circles meet at \(A\) and at its reflection \(A'\) across \(OB\). Their overlapping portion on the circle centered at \(B\) is the arc from \(A\) to \(A'\) facing \(O\). Since \(\angle ABO=\theta/2\), this successful arc has central angle \(\theta\).

Let \(\phi\in[-\pi,\pi)\) be the signed angle of the third jump measured from the direction \(BO\). The successful directions are precisely
\[
-\frac{\theta}{2}\le\phi\le\frac{\theta}{2}.
\]
The third direction remains uniform after choosing this reference direction, because it is independent of the first two jumps. Thus \((\theta,\phi)\) is uniform in a rectangle of width \(\pi\) and height \(2\pi\). The successful region is a triangle with height \(\pi\) and base \(\pi\), so its area is \(\pi^2/2\).

The endpoint cases have probability zero: when \(\theta=0\), only a directly backward third jump succeeds; when \(\theta=\pi\), the frog is already back at \(O\), so every third jump succeeds. Including these cases and the accepted arc boundaries does not change the area ratio. Therefore
\[
P=\frac{\pi^2/2}{2\pi^2}=\boxed{\frac14},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
